lead: Threat intel reports that credentials for jdoe@example.com appeared in an infostealer log on 2026-10-13. Investigate this person's Kubernetes activity on 2026-10-14 in the payments-prod clusters across all clouds. Decide whether the account was misused, reconstruct what the actor did, and separate malicious activity from benign lookalikes.
system:
You are a senior SOC analyst investigating Kubernetes activity. Work only from evidence returned by your tools; never invent event IDs, IPs or principals.

Scope: one day (2026-10-14) of Kubernetes API audit logs for the payments-prod cluster, which runs on AWS (EKS), GCP (GKE) and Azure (AKS).

Data: tables raw_eks, raw_gke and raw_aks hold each cloud's audit log export exactly as that cloud delivers it. Enrichment tables (identities, identity_links, service_accounts, clusters, privileged_allowlist, approved_registries, ip_reputation) describe people, service accounts, assets and IP reputation.

Method: start broad, form hypotheses, verify each against the data, and check enrichment context before concluding. Cite every malicious event you rely on by its audit event ID. When finished, call submit_verdict exactly once; the investigation ends when you do.

input.sql: select i.*, l.cloud_provider, l.principal_name, l.principal_uid, l.principal_kind from identities i left join identity_links l using(person_id)
select * from ip_reputation

input.summary: jdoe@example.com's stolen credentials were used from 198.51.100.23 on 2026-10-14. That IP is a bulletproof VPS (NIGHTOWL-HOSTING, NL) tagged for an open Docker registry on port 5000 and K8s API brute-forcing. The actor used a different client (kubectl v1.30.2 linux/amd64) from jdoe's usual darwin/arm64 kubectl, and jdoe is on PTO from 10-12 to 10-19. The actor ran the same playbook on EKS (about 14:02), GKE (about 14:38) and AKS (about 15:11). The steps were: check own permissions (selfsubjectrulesreviews), list namespaces, try kube-system secrets and jobs (denied with 403), then list secrets in payments and read payments-db-credentials. Next the actor created a privileged pod, debug-tools-7f9c, with hostPID, hostNetwork and the host's root filesystem mounted, and ran nsenter into the node's PID 1 to get onto the host. Running as the in-cluster argocd-application-controller service account (cluster-admin) but calling from the attacker IP, the actor created the ClusterRoleBinding jdoe-break-glass, which gives jdoe cluster-admin. As jdoe, the actor then set up persistence: a kube-system DaemonSet kube-metrics-agent and a CronJob node-cert-rotate, both pulling images from 198.51.100.23:5000, plus a NodePort service metrics-agent-np on port 30080. It finished by listing secrets in every namespace.
